before.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, and the frontierism Canadian historians took from it, criticised as environmental determinism; the frontier recast as a dependent of the metropolis (1954)
before.evidence_note: His own words. 'Frontierism, Metropolitanism, and Canadian History' (1954), read in full. He summarises Turner's thesis that 'the greatest formative influence' in American history had been 'the open frontier, the hither edge of free land' (p. 6) and judges: 'This was environmental determinism at its most forthright. The wilderness and the men it produced had made America' (p. 7). Against it he sets the metropolitan reading: the frontier's culture 'originally stems from a metropolitan community; at root, learning and ideas radiate from there—and thus is Turner answered' (p. 18); 'the frontier, far from being essentially independent and self-reliant, is in the largest sense a dependent' (p. 18); and 'the functioning of metropolitanism may do more to explain the course of Canadian history than concepts of frontierism borrowed from the United States and set forth before the significance of the modern metropolis was clear' (p. 20). 'At any rate, frontierism, along with earlier schools and approaches, has had its use and its day' (p. 21). His qualifications are kept: 'Defenders of Turner might claim that he had not proposed a frontier hypothesis as the only key to American history' (p. 7); the frontier thesis 'proper' was never 'adopted as fully or dogmatically in Canada as it was in the United States—and there, of course, it has long been the subject of qualification and criticism' (p. 1); Canadian environmentalists took over 'the general approach and mood of Turner and company ... rather than the precise frontier thesis, which received little direct application in Canada' (p. 6). He draws on American critics of Turner (Hayes, Fox, Schlesinger Jr.; pp. 7–8) and on Canadian ones (McDougall 1929, Stanley 1940; p. 10, n. 21). The critique is therefore aimed at Turner's thesis and above all at its Canadian adaptation; the Canadian historians he names sit in cdn_national_tradition and are covered by edge 1. In-period reading: Davis (1985, p. 95, read) calls the article 'Conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner'. Davis (p. 109) also quotes Careless on television saying of Turner's thesis that 'like any view of history which gets oversimplified, overpopularized, it becomes untrue; it becomes a myth' (undated, a quoted-in witness). No reply by a Turnerian historian was found or read.

before.relationship: Turner's frontier thesis, as taken up by Canadian historians in the 1930s and 1940s, rejected as an imported 'continental revelation' that Canadian history would not fit (1957)
before.evidence_note: His own text, the 1957 CHA presidential address (read in full). Canadian historians had 'accepted, for historical purposes, the two highly fashionable political theories which dominated the thought of the inter-war and war years': 'the Marxian doctrine of the class struggle' and 'the Frontier Theory' (p. 6). Of the second: 'Turner ... fixed upon the movement of settlement across the continent as the most important fact in its history'; 'the source of creative inspiration and action was found not at the centre, but at the periphery, of western culture' (p. 8). Applied to Canada, 'painful difficulties were immediately encountered': the frontier's progress 'had been evidently modified by all sorts of extraneous and unnatural things such as railways, efficient police, governmental supervision'; in 1837 'the rebels had come, not from the frontier, but from the older settled parts of the province'; yet its believers 'kept insisting that Canadian democracy was "forest-born"' (p. 9). He ends: historians bought 'a couple of suits of imported intellectual reach-me-downs' and a new generation would show 'less deference for imported theories of historical change and more respect for the manifold facts of Canadian experience' (p. 12). The critique inverts his own Laurentian premise, that change radiates from the centre. Limits: the address is a polemic and names no Canadian frontierist; Turner is not quoted beyond the phrases Creighton cites, and the atlas's own reading of Turner (progressive/multiple_hypotheses) shows him advocating multiple hypotheses rather than a single doctrine. Context: Careless's 1954 CHR article, unread here, was 'conceived in part as an obituary for the frontier thesis of Frederick Jackson Turner' (Davis 1985, p. 95). No in-period reply to the address was looked for.
